lesson.label: 📖 Bài học chính
lesson.title: 1. Minimalist vs. Maximalist
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Sophie is helping her friend Ella move into a new flat. They’re carrying boxes up the stairs.*
lines: Careful with that one. It’s full of plants.
Another one? Ella, this is the fourth box of plants.
I know. I’m **a bit of a hoarder**. I’ve **accumulated** a lot of **stuff** over the years.
“A lot” is **an understatement**. You’ve got more cushions than chairs.
They make the place feel **cosy**. I like **being surrounded by** things that mean something to me: photos, books, **little knick-knacks** from trips.
I get that. I’m **the complete opposite**. My flat’s almost empty: a sofa, a table, a bed, and **that’s about it**.
I know. It looks like **a show home**. Doesn’t it feel a bit cold?
Not to me. I find **clutter** really stressful. When everything’s **tidy**, I can actually relax. Plus, cleaning takes ten minutes.
That’s the one thing I’m jealous of. Dusting all my shelves **takes forever**. It’s **a real pain**.
Last year, I had a big **declutter**. I **gave away** half my clothes, and honestly, I don’t miss any of them. **Less is more.**
I could never do that. Most of my things have **sentimental value**. I still have concert tickets from 2015. I just **can’t bring myself to** throw them away.
That’s the difference between us. You keep things for the memories. **I’d rather** keep the memories **than** the stuff.
**Fair point.** But **bare** white walls just make me sad. A home should **feel lived-in**.
So where’s all this going to go? Your new place isn’t exactly huge, and there’s **hardly any storage space**.
I’ll **make it work**. A few more shelves, some hooks on the walls…
Or you could **get rid of** a few cushions.

lesson.title: 2. Home, sweet home
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Ben and Hannah are colleagues. On Monday, Hannah asks Ben about the flat he moved into at the weekend.*
lines: How’s the new place? You moved last weekend, didn’t you?
Yeah. It’s only **a studio**, and it’s a bit small, but **it’s all mine**. After three years of **sharing a house** with four **flatmates**, it feels amazing.
No more queuing for the bathroom.
And no more arguments about whose turn it is to **take out the bins**. I finally **have the place to myself**, and I can **come and go as I please**.
Isn’t it a bit lonely, though?
Sometimes, in the evenings. But I’m enjoying **the peace and quiet**, and I **invite friends over** more often now.
What about the rent? I bet it’s not cheap.
That’s **the downside**. I’m paying almost twice as much as before, and **the bills are all on me** now.
That’s why I’m thinking of **moving back in with** my parents for a year.
Really? Would you be OK with that?
I’m not sure. I’d **lose some of my freedom**, obviously, and my mum would ask where I’m going every time I leave the house. But I could **save for a deposit**.
That sounds like a good plan. Renting is so expensive these days. My old landlord **put the rent up** twice last year. By the way, are you looking at flats or houses?
Flats, probably. A house with a garden would be lovely, but it’s **out of my price range**, unless I move out to **the suburbs**. And then **the commute** would be awful.
Well, if you ever need a break from your parents, you’re welcome to **crash on my sofa**.

homework.title: Part 1: Vocab check
homework.instructions: Fill in each blank with a phrase from the word bank. Use each phrase once.
homework.context: Jess and Tom are moving in together next month. They’re at Tom’s flat, deciding what to take with them.
lines: Tom, how many mugs do you actually have?
About thirty, I think. I’ve {accumulated} a lot of stuff since I moved here.
“A lot” is {an understatement}. This cupboard is full of mugs, and the shelves are covered in little {knick-knacks} from your trips.
I know. I keep meaning to throw some things away, but I just {can’t bring myself to} do it. Most of them have {sentimental value}.
I get that. But our new flat is half the size of this one, and there’s {hardly any} storage space.
Can’t we just buy more shelves? I don’t want our place to look like {a show home}, with nothing on the walls.
Neither do I. A home should {feel lived-in}. But we need to be realistic. Why don’t we have a big {declutter} this weekend? Anything we don’t need, we can give away.
Fair enough. Remind me why we didn’t look for a bigger place?
Because anything with two bedrooms in the city centre was {out of our price range}, unless we moved out to the suburbs.
Right. And neither of us wanted a long commute.
Exactly. So, let’s start with the mugs.

homework.title: Part 2: Listening
homework.intro: Listen to part of a podcast about a woman who moved back in with her parents, then do Parts A and B.
homework.podcast: 🎧 Money Matters: back to my childhood bedroom

script.text: Welcome back to Money Matters. Today's guest is Rachel, who moved back in with her parents at the age of twenty-nine.

People are always surprised when I tell them. For most of my twenties, I rented a flat in the city with two ==friends==. I loved it. We had a great social life, and I could come and go as I pleased. But ==every year, our landlord put the rent up==, and I realised I was saving almost ==nothing==.
So last year, I made a decision. I moved back into my childhood bedroom, with a plan to save enough for a deposit in two years.

The first few months were harder than I expected. ==It wasn't the small room. It was the questions. My mum wanted to know where I was going==, who I was meeting and what time I'd be home. I felt like a ==teenager== again. We had a few arguments, and in the end, ==we sat down and agreed on some ground rules==. Now, I let her know if I'll be back late, and she doesn't ask for the details.

Financially, it's been amazing. I pay my parents a small amount each month for food and bills, which is less than a ==quarter== of my old rent. ==I've already saved more than I did in five years of renting.==

There are downsides, of course. My ==commute== is longer, because my parents live in the suburbs, and I don't invite friends over as often as I'd like. But ==I've also got to know my parents as an adult, which I didn't expect==. My dad and I cook ==dinner together== twice a week now.
Would I recommend it? ==If you get on well with your family and you set clear boundaries, absolutely.== Just don't expect it to be easy.

questions.q: Why did Rachel decide to move back home?
options: She didn’t get on with her flatmates.
The rising rent made it hard to save.
Her parents asked her to come back.
questions.why: “Every year, our landlord put the rent up, and I realised I was saving almost nothing.”

questions.q: What did Rachel find most difficult at first?
options: Living in a small bedroom again
Her mum wanting to know about her plans
Having to pay her parents every month
questions.why: “It wasn’t the small room. It was the questions.”

questions.q: How did they solve the problem?
options: Rachel promised to always come home early.
Her mum stopped asking any questions at all.
They agreed on some rules together.
questions.why: “We sat down and agreed on some ground rules.”

questions.q: What do we learn about Rachel’s savings?
options: She now pays her parents exactly a quarter of her old rent.
She has saved more in about a year than in five years of renting.
She has already saved enough for a deposit.
questions.why: She moved last year and has “already saved more than I did in five years of renting.” She pays less than a quarter, not exactly a quarter.

questions.q: What unexpected benefit does Rachel mention?
options: A closer relationship with her parents
More time to see her friends
questions.why: “I’ve also got to know my parents as an adult, which I didn’t expect.”

questions.q: Who would Rachel recommend moving back home to?
options: People who can’t afford to rent
People who are good at saving money
People who have a good relationship with their family
questions.why: “If you get on well with your family and you set clear boundaries, absolutely.”

homework.title: Part 2B: Complete the summary
homework.instructions: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each blank.
homework.text: For most of her twenties, Rachel rented a flat with two {friends}. Because the rent kept going up, she was saving almost {nothing}. At first, living at home made her feel like a {teenager} again, so she and her mum agreed on some {ground rules|rules}. She now pays her parents less than a {quarter} of her old rent. The main downsides are a longer {commute} and inviting friends over less often. However, she now cooks {dinner together|dinner} with her dad twice a week.
